review.statement: Fix a finite universal two-qubit gate set G. At each of m(n) = ⌈Cn^c⌉ steps, independently draw a uniform gate from G and a uniform qubit pair. Does there exist C,c > 0, fixed before choosing the adversary, such that every polynomial-time quantum algorithm with adaptive forward-only oracle access has negligible distinguishing advantage between the resulting n-qubit unitary and a Haar draw? One unitary is sampled and reused throughout each experiment. Negligible means that for each fixed adversary and every k > 0, its absolute acceptance-probability gap is eventually below n⁻ᵏ. [A27](https://openquantumproblems.com/p/A27)
review.significance: This asks whether repeated random two-qubit interactions can produce cryptographic pseudorandomness. In the same all-to-all geometry, Corollary 1.7 gives a multiplicative-error t-design upper bound of O(n(nt + log(1/ε))(log t)^4) gates for Haar two-qubit draws, with similar scaling for fixed universal gate distributions as discussed immediately after the corollary. For a fixed finite G, a support-rank calculation gives a necessary Ω(nt/log n) gates for a multiplicative-error t-design with ε < 1 and 2 ≤ t ≤ poly(n). The two bounds concern design formation. They leave the fixed-size computational question open. [Chen et al., Corollary 1.7](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.07478)
review.settlement_test: A positive result gives one pair C,c and proves negligible advantage for every polynomial-time forward-query adversary. A negative result for the fixed G gives, for every C,c, a polynomial-time forward-query adversary with inverse-polynomial advantage on infinitely many n. For a claim covering every finite universal G, one admissible gate set with such a negative result would refute that claim.
review.aliases: Quantum Gowers conjecture. Bostanci et al., TQC 2025 Conjecture 1, call it “Random quantum circuits give rise to pseudorandom unitaries” and state a threshold m ≥ C_G n^c. A27 asks for one fixed size schedule. The October 2026 Conjecture 6.1 proposes a sufficient condition based on linear-order designs for i.i.d. local gates. [TQC Conjecture 1](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol350-tqc2025/LIPIcs.TQC.2025.9/LIPIcs.TQC.2025.9.pdf) [October 2026 Conjecture 6.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.02100v1)
review.attempt: Checked the October 2026 arXiv version record and Theorems 1.3–1.4 and Conjecture 6.1. Theorem 1.3 uses engineered gate distributions that depend on n and the chosen fixed design order. After O_t(n² log² n) steps it achieves that design order, yet O_t(log² n) parallel forward queries distinguish it with constant advantage. Theorem 1.4 uses a separate structured phase layer. Checked the scope of the September distinctness paper, the original TQC Conjecture 1, and the design upper bound in Corollary 1.7. Searched the exact title and quantum Gowers alias for later resolutions and found none for A27’s sampler. For the design lower bound, each circuit contributes one pure t-copy output from |0ⁿ⟩, so the averaged output has rank at most (|G|n(n−1))^m. The Haar average has full rank binom(2^n+t−1,t) on the symmetric subspace. A multiplicative lower inequality with ε < 1 forces at least that rank. Taking logs gives Ω(nt/log n). [October 2026 paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.02100v1) [Distinctness paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.03065v1) [Design bound](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.07478)
review.remaining_obligation: Test one specialization of Conjecture 6.1. Fix an inverse-closed finite universal G with algebraic entries and choose one polynomial size schedule that gives a negligible-error t = n design under the all-to-all walk. Prove that every polynomial-size parallel forward-query test on that schedule has negligible advantage, or exhibit one such test with inverse-polynomial advantage. A parallel-security proof would still leave adaptive security to establish. A distinguisher for that schedule would leave other polynomial schedules open.
review.human_brief: A qubit is a two-level quantum system. Pick two qubits at random, apply a random gate from a fixed menu, and repeat. An observer can run the same hidden circuit on chosen inputs. Haar randomness draws the entire transformation uniformly. For a toy example, start three qubits in |000⟩ and apply one gate. The untouched qubit stays at zero, so measuring 111 has probability zero. For a Haar draw the average probability is 1/8 because all eight outcomes are symmetric. If the lab can coherently run two copies of the same device side by side, the next test can use an entangled input across the copies, exposing correlations a single run cannot measure.
